pages.text: This is a story set in a possible future. In 2064, four Ghanaian students aged fifteen were on a week-long training flight aboard Sankofa Station, a small laboratory about 400 km above Earth. Kwamena was crew leader, Salma the engineer, Mina the medic, and Atta the navigator. Commander Danquah and Pilot Ofosu had taken a shuttle for a short repair job and would be back in ninety minutes.
sentences: This is a story set in a possible future.
In 2064, four Ghanaian students aged fifteen were on a week-long training flight aboard Sankofa Station, a small laboratory about 400 km above Earth.
Kwamena was crew leader, Salma the engineer, Mina the medic, and Atta the navigator.
Commander Danquah and Pilot Ofosu had taken a shuttle for a short repair job and would be back in ninety minutes.
pages.alt: Four teenage cadets in flight suits float in a small station with Earth in the window.

pages.text: Ninety minutes passed. A message crackled: ‘Shuttle damaged… docking delayed… up to seven days… conserve power…’ Then silence. At the same moment, half the lights went out. ‘Solar array fault,’ said Salma, reading a panel. ‘Half our power is gone.’ Mina’s hands shook. Kwamena took a breath. ‘First, we stay calm. Second, we make a plan, with numbers.’
sentences: Ninety minutes passed.
A message crackled: ‘Shuttle damaged… docking delayed… up to seven days… conserve power…’ Then silence.
At the same moment, half the lights went out.
‘Solar array fault,’ said Salma, reading a panel.
‘Half our power is gone.’ Mina’s hands shook.
Kwamena took a breath.
‘First, we stay calm.
Second, we make a plan, with numbers.’
pages.alt: The cabin lights dim and four cadets look at a flickering panel.

pages.text: Atta found the supply log. Water: 60 kg. Emergency oxygen: 26 kg. Food: 24 kg. Mina read from her notes: ‘Each person needs up to about 1 kg of oxygen, about 3 kg of drinking water and about 0.8 kg of food a day.’ For four people that is 4 kg of oxygen, 12 kg of water and 3.2 kg of food every day.
sentences: Atta found the supply log.
Water: 60 kg.
Emergency oxygen: 26 kg.
Food: 24 kg.

Mina read from her notes: ‘Each person needs up to about 1 kg of oxygen, about 3 kg of drinking water and about 0.8 kg of food a day.’ For four people that is 4 kg of oxygen, 12 kg of water and 3.2 kg of food every day.
pages.alt: A cadet reads numbers from a supply log while another writes them on a board.

pages.text: Salma did the sums. Oxygen: 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 days. Water: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 days. Food: 24 ÷ 3.2 = 7.5 days. ‘Water is our limit,’ said Atta. ‘Five days. But help may take seven.’ Mina spoke. ‘A person needs at least a little over 2 kg of drinking water a day. If we cut washing water to almost nothing and each drink 2.5 kg, we use 10 kg a day, and 60 ÷ 10 = 6 days.’ ‘Still one day short,’ said Atta.
sentences: Salma did the sums.
Oxygen: 26 ÷ 4 = 6.5 days.
Water: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 days.
Food: 24 ÷ 3.2 = 7.5 days.
‘Water is our limit,’ said Atta.
‘Five days.
But help may take seven.’ Mina spoke.
‘A person needs at least a little over 2 kg of drinking water a day.
If we cut washing water to almost nothing and each drink 2.5 kg, we use 10 kg a day, and 60 ÷ 10 = 6 days.’ ‘Still one day short,’ said Atta.
pages.alt: The cadets write three sums on a whiteboard and circle the smallest answer.

pages.text: Salma had an idea. ‘The cabin air carries water from our breath and sweat. The air dryer can still run on the battery. If it recovers about 4 kg of water a day, we only need to supply 10 − 4 = 6 kg.’ She worked it out. ‘60 ÷ 6 = 10 days. That is more than seven, and we would have three days to spare.’ Nobody cheered, but everyone breathed more easily.
sentences: Salma had an idea.
‘The cabin air carries water from our breath and sweat.
The air dryer can still run on the battery.
If it recovers about 4 kg of water a day, we only need to supply 10 − 4 = 6 kg.’ She worked it out.
That is more than seven, and we would have three days to spare.’ Nobody cheered, but everyone breathed more easily.
pages.alt: A cadet shows a diagram of the air dryer collecting water droplets.

pages.text: Power was the next problem. With half the solar panels gone, they had to choose what to switch off. They kept the air fans, the carbon dioxide scrubber, the air dryer and the radio. They switched off the extra lights, the games screen and the heater to the empty lab. They also rested more, because resting uses less oxygen. ‘Every choice has a cost,’ said Mina. ‘We write each one down.’
sentences: Power was the next problem.
With half the solar panels gone, they had to choose what to switch off.
They kept the air fans, the carbon dioxide scrubber, the air dryer and the radio.
They switched off the extra lights, the games screen and the heater to the empty lab.
They also rested more, because resting uses less oxygen.
‘Every choice has a cost,’ said Mina.
‘We write each one down.’
pages.alt: The cadets switch off non-essential panels, leaving four green lights.

pages.text: Every 92 minutes, the station completed one orbit of Earth, so they saw about sixteen sunrises a day. Atta worked out when they passed over Africa and could be heard by the ground station. They sent the same short message each time: Four crew safe. Water: ten days. Air: good. Power: half. Atta thought of GhanaSat-1, a tiny cube satellite built by engineers at All Nations University and released from the space station in 2017. ‘If a small team could do that,’ he said, ‘we can send a message.’

Atta thought of GhanaSat-1, a tiny cube satellite built by engineers at All Nations University and released from the space station in 2017.
‘If a small team could do that,’ he said, ‘we can send a message.’
pages.alt: Atta types a message at a radio panel with Earth glowing in the window behind him.

pages.text: On the sixth day the radio crackled: ‘Sankofa Station, this is Commander Danquah. We heard you. We are two hours from docking.’ The cadets cheered quietly, to save energy. When the shuttle docked, the Commander checked the log: every sum and every decision. ‘You did what trained crews do,’ he said. ‘You stayed calm, counted, shared the work and told the truth about the numbers.’ Kwamena smiled. ‘And we only argued twice,’ he said. The end.

‘You stayed calm, counted, shared the work and told the truth about the numbers.’ Kwamena smiled.
‘And we only argued twice,’ he said.
The end.
pages.alt: The shuttle docks as four cadets float together smiling by the window.

activities.question: Which resource was the cadets’ limit at first?
activities.explanation: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 days, which is less than oxygen (6.5) or food (7.5).

activities.question: How did recovering water from the cabin air change the plan?
options: The supply lasted 10 days instead of 6

activities.prompt: Power is limited. What should the cadets keep switched on, and what could they switch off?
options: Keep air fans, scrubber, dryer, radio; switch off extra lights and games
Keep the games screen and switch off the scrubber

activities.definition: A device that removes carbon dioxide from the air.

activities.question: About how many sunrises do astronauts on the space station see each day?
activities.explanation: Each orbit takes about 92 minutes, so there are around 16 sunrises a day.

activities.prompt: Put the cadets’ plan in order.
items: Stay calm and decide to plan with numbers.
Calculate how long each supply lasts.
Find ways to stretch the limiting supply.
Decide what power to keep and what to switch off.
